title: Farewell to Manzanar: A True Story of Japanese American Experience During and After the World War II Internment
author: Jeanne Wakatsuki Houston and James D. Houston
target_audience: Students studying American history and World War II
Readers interested in memoirs and autobiographies
Individuals seeking to understand Japanese American experiences
Educators teaching about racism, civil rights, or internment camps
Anyone interested in stories of resilience and identity
core_themes: Memory, trauma, and coming of age
primary_purpose: To provide a deeply personal, firsthand account of the Japanese American internment experience during World War II through the eyes of a young girl, exploring the effects on her family, identity, and future, and to shed light on this chapter of American history.

structure_format.organization: Divided into short chapters recounting chronological events from pre-internment to post-war
features: Descriptions of family and community life

key_concepts_lessons: Institutional racism can have profound, generational effects on individuals and families.
Internment camps were dehumanizing yet fostered unique forms of community adaptation and survival.
National crises can provoke fear-based policies targeting minority groups.
The search for identity intensifies under external pressures and cultural conflict.
Resilience is built through family bonds and adaptation to injustice.
Collective memory and personal narrative are powerful tools for healing and teaching.
notable_features: First widely read memoir about Japanese American internment
Blends personal narrative with historical background
Used in schools and universities for its accessibility and perspective
Explores both the emotional and societal aftermath for internees
cultural_historical_context: Published three decades after World War II, 'Farewell to Manzanar' broke cultural silence about Japanese American internment. The 1970s was a period of increased interest in civil rights, and the book contributed to national discussions about racism, injustice, memory, and reconciliation.
reception_impact: Acclaimed for bringing visibility to Japanese American wartime experiences
Instrumental in personalizing historical events often omitted from major narratives
Credited with influencing later redress efforts and reparations for Japanese Americans
Highly regarded for its honest, accessible prose and emotional resonance
comparable_titles: They Called Us Enemy by George Takei
When the Emperor Was Divine by Julie Otsuka
